question: Shivaji was coronated with full Vedic rites at Raigad in the year:
In the Third Battle of Panipat (1761), the Marathas suffered a disastrous defeat at the hands of:

Match List I with List II:

| List I | List II |
|---|---|
| A. Chhatrapati Shivaji's coronation at Raigad | 1. 1818 |
| B. Maratha defeat in the Battle of Panipat | 2. 1771 |
| C. Recapture of Delhi under Mahadji Shinde | 3. 1761 |
| D. Third Anglo-Maratha War, end of Maratha power | 4. 1674 |
Check every claim in this statement and explanation against NCERT; list any claim NCERT does not support or contradicts.
text:
Chhatrapati Shivaji was coronated with full Vedic rites at Raigad in 1674; his formal title after the coronation was 'Shri Raja Shiva Chhatrapati'.
He had a council of eight ministers to assist him with administration. Later, the Peshwa (a Persian term for 'prime minister') wielded great influence, even over the Chhatrapati himself.
The Marathas levied chauth (25 per cent) and sardeshmukhi (an additional 10 per cent to chauth) from provinces that were not directly under them.
In their northward expansion the Marathas fought the Afghans: Ahmad Shah Abdali defeated them in the Third Battle of Panipat (1761), a disastrous defeat, but they quickly recovered during the time of Peshwa Madhavrao I, and under Mahadji Shinde they recaptured Delhi in 1771.

Two Maratha years carry most questions: 1674 (coronation at Raigad) and 1761 (Third Panipat, fought against the Afghans under Ahmad Shah Abdali, NOT against the Mughals or the British). NCERT stresses the recovery: the Marathas quickly recovered and retook Delhi in 1771, and their power ended only with the Third Anglo-Maratha War (1818). Note Panipat's three battles: 1526, 1556, 1761.

question: According to an Asokan inscription quoted in NCERT, the Kalingas were conquered when Ashoka had been ruling for:
Most of Ashoka's inscriptions are written in:

Consider the following statements about Ashoka:

1. He conquered Kalinga (present-day coastal Orissa).
2. He was the first ruler to inscribe his messages to his subjects and officials on stone surfaces, including polished pillars.
3. James Prinsep deciphered Asokan Brahmi in 1838.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
Check every claim in this statement and explanation against NCERT; list any claim NCERT does not support or contradicts.
text:
Ashoka conquered Kalinga (present-day coastal Orissa); his inscription says this happened when he had been ruling for eight years, and that afterwards he devoted himself to the study of Dhamma and to instructing people in it.
Ashoka was the first ruler to inscribe his messages to his subjects and officials on stone surfaces — natural rocks as well as polished pillars.
Most Asokan inscriptions are in the Prakrit language and most of them are written in the Brahmi script; those in the north-west are in Aramaic and Greek, and some Prakrit inscriptions in the north-west are in Kharosthi.
James Prinsep was able to decipher Asokan Brahmi in 1838.

Three Ashoka questions rotate: Kalinga (conquered when he had been ruling for eight years; NCERT gives no calendar year for it), the language-script pair (Prakrit in Brahmi, with Kharosthi, Aramaic and Greek in the north-west), and the decipherment by James Prinsep (1838). NCERT dates Asoka c. 272/268-231 BCE.

question: The Second Battle of Panipat (1556) was fought between Akbar's forces and:
Akbar established a 'house of translation', where major Sanskrit texts were translated into Persian, in which city built by him near Agra?
Which of the following pairs of battle and year is correctly matched?
Check every claim in this statement and explanation against NCERT; list any claim NCERT does not support or contradicts.
text:
Akbar was declared emperor at the age of 13 upon his father Humayun's accidental death; his long reign lasted almost 50 years (1556 to his death in 1605).
In the Second Battle of Panipat (1556), Himu (Hemu), who had captured Delhi, was injured on the battlefield when confronted by Akbar; he was captured and beheaded, and Akbar reclaimed Delhi for the Mughals.
Akbar abolished the jizya and promoted the doctrine of sulh-i-kul ('peace with all', or tolerance of all faiths). At Fatehpur Sikri, a city he built near Agra, he established a 'house of translation' where Sanskrit texts such as the Mahabharata (Razmnama) were translated into Persian.
Todar Mal, his finance minister, introduced an efficient revenue system based on detailed surveys; Akbar also instituted the mansabdari system, in which mansabdars (officers) were expected, according to their mansab (rank), to maintain a precise number of elephants, horses, camels and troops for the state.

Akbar's anchors in NCERT: emperor from 1556 (reign 1556-1605), Second Panipat 1556 against Himu (Hemu), Haldighati 1576. Do not swap Panipat II (Akbar's decisive victory over Himu, 1556) with Panipat I (Babur's victory over Ibrahim Lodi, 1526).

question:
Match List I with List II:

| List I | List II |
|---|---|
| A. Lumbini | 1. Where the Buddha attained nibbana |
| B. Bodh Gaya | 2. Where the Buddha was born |
| C. Sarnath | 3. Where the Buddha gave his first sermon |
| D. Kusinagara | 4. Where the Buddha attained enlightenment |
The Buddha gave his first sermon at:
According to NCERT, after the Buddha's death his teachings were compiled by his disciples at a council of 'elders' held at:
Check every claim in this statement and explanation against NCERT; list any claim NCERT does not support or contradicts.
text:
The Buddha taught orally, and none of his speeches were written down during his lifetime. After his death (c. fifth-fourth century BCE) his teachings were compiled by his disciples at a council of 'elders' or senior monks at Vesali (Pali for Vaishali, in present-day Bihar). These compilations were known as Tipitaka, 'three baskets': the Vinaya Pitaka, the Sutta Pitaka and the Abhidhamma Pitaka.
Four places in the Buddha's life came to be regarded as sacred: Lumbini (where he was born), Bodh Gaya (enlightenment), Sarnath (first sermon) and Kusinagara (nibbana). About 200 years after the Buddha, Asoka erected a pillar at Lumbini.
By the first century CE there is evidence of changes in Buddhist ideas: the new way of thinking was called Mahayana ('great vehicle'), and its followers described the older tradition as Hinayana ('lesser vehicle'), while followers of the older tradition called themselves theravadins.

Match the four places with birth, enlightenment, first sermon and nibbana (death) — a favourite question. NCERT names the council at Vaishali (Vesali) as the place where the Buddha's teachings were compiled after his death into the Tipitaka.

question: The practice of sati was banned in the year:
Under Lord Dalhousie's Doctrine of Lapse, the kingdom of Satara was annexed in:
Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
Check every claim in this statement and explanation against NCERT; list any claim NCERT does not support or contradicts.
text:
Raja Rammohun Roy began a campaign against the practice of sati, and in 1829 sati was banned.
Following Macaulay's minute, the English Education Act of 1835 was introduced: English was made the medium of instruction for higher education. In 1854 Wood's Despatch, issued by Charles Wood, President of the Board of Control, outlined the educational policy to be followed in India.
Lord Dalhousie, Governor-General from 1848 to 1856, devised the Doctrine of Lapse: if an Indian ruler died without a male heir, his kingdom would 'lapse' and become part of Company territory. Kingdoms annexed by applying it: Satara (1848), Sambalpur (1850), Udaipur (1852), Nagpur (1853) and Jhansi (1854).
In 1856 the Company also took over Awadh, on the argument that the Nawab misgoverned it.

Pair the policy with its year: sati banned 1829; English Education Act 1835 (Macaulay's minute); Wood's Despatch 1854; Doctrine of Lapse under Dalhousie (1848-56), beginning with Satara (1848). NCERT notes that the humiliating way the Nawab of Awadh was deposed enraged the people of Awadh, who joined the great revolt of 1857.

question: According to NCERT, Subhas Chandra Bose formed the Indian National Army and declared the Azad Hind government in 1943 at:
According to NCERT Class 8, who formed the Indian National Army in Singapore in 1943 from Indian prisoners of war and volunteers?

Consider the following statements about the INA:

1. It was formed from Indian prisoners of war and volunteers in Singapore in 1943.
2. It fought alongside the Japanese army in Burma and north-eastern India.
3. It was formed in Berlin in 1941.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
Check every claim in this statement and explanation against NCERT; list any claim NCERT does not support or contradicts.
text:
Subhas Chandra Bose escaped house arrest in India in early 1941 and travelled through Afghanistan and Russia to Germany, where he spent almost two years seeking support from anti-British forces. He then travelled to Indonesia, Japan and finally Singapore in 1943, where he formed the Indian National Army (INA) from Indian prisoners of war and volunteers and declared the formation of the Azad Hind ('free India') government.
The INA fought alongside the Japanese army in Burma and north-eastern India, particularly Manipur and Nagaland; in 1944 it tried to enter India through Imphal and Kohima, but it was militarily defeated and failed to establish a base in India.
INA members were imprisoned and tried, and people across the country, from all walks of life, took part in the movement against the INA trials.
In February 1946 a mutiny started in the Royal Indian Navy in Bombay, a month after a mutiny in the Royal Indian Air Force.

According to NCERT, the INA was formed by Subhas Chandra Bose in Singapore in 1943 from Indian prisoners of war and volunteers, together with the declaration of the Azad Hind government; before that, in early 1941, he had escaped house arrest in India and reached Germany.

question: The Congress split between Moderates and Nationalists at the session of:
The Purna Swaraj resolution was adopted in 1929, with the Congress under the presidentship of:

Match List I with List II:

| List I | List II |
|---|---|
| A. Surat 1907 | 1. Non-Cooperation Movement formally launched |
| B. Lucknow 1916 | 2. Resolution to fight for Purna Swaraj |
| C. Nagpur 1920 | 3. Split between Moderates and Nationalists |
| D. Lahore 1929 | 4. Lucknow Pact with the Muslim League |
Check every claim in this statement and explanation against NCERT; list any claim NCERT does not support or contradicts.
text:
1885 Bombay — the first session of the Indian National Congress; Womesh Chunder Bonnerjee was elected its first president, and seventy-two delegates attended.
1907 Surat — the Congress split between Moderates and Nationalists.
1916 Lucknow — the Congress and the All-India Muslim League reached the Lucknow Pact; under it the Congress accepted separate electorates for Muslims.
1920 Nagpur — after Tilak's death (August 1920) Gandhi became the undisputed mass leader, and the Congress formally launched the Non-Cooperation Movement at its Nagpur session in December.
1929 Lahore — the Congress resolved to fight for Purna Swaraj (complete independence) under the presidentship of Jawaharlal Nehru; 'Independence Day' was observed on 26 January 1930.

Session questions come in triples: year, place, significance. The highest-yield chain: Surat split (1907) -> Lucknow Pact with the Muslim League (1916) -> Nagpur Non-Cooperation (1920) -> Lahore Purna Swaraj under Nehru (1929). The Lahore president is asked separately.

question: The British government conceded the Muslim League's demand for separate electorates for Muslims in:
The Government of India Act of 1935 prescribed:
options: Transfer of the Company's powers to the Crown

question:
Match List I with List II:

| List I | List II |
|---|---|
| A. Regulating Act, 1773 | 1. Provincial autonomy prescribed |
| B. Act of 1858 | 2. A new Supreme Court established |
| C. Concession of 1909 | 3. Powers of the Company transferred to the Crown; Governor-General titled Viceroy |
| D. Government of India Act, 1935 | 4. Separate electorates for Muslims |
Check every claim in this statement and explanation against NCERT; list any claim NCERT does not support or contradicts.
text:
Under the Regulating Act of 1773 a new Supreme Court was established; Warren Hastings (Governor-General from 1773 to 1785) was the first Governor-General, the supreme head of the administration.
The Act of 1858 transferred the powers of the East India Company to the British Crown; a member of the British Cabinet became Secretary of State for India, with an India Council to advise him, and the Governor-General of India was given the title of Viceroy.
The Muslim League (founded 1906) desired separate electorates for Muslims, a demand conceded by the government in 1909; some council seats were reserved for Muslims, elected by Muslim voters.
The Montague-Chelmsford Reforms of 1919 allowed some form of representation in provincial legislative assemblies.
The Government of India Act of 1935 prescribed provincial autonomy, and elections to the provincial legislatures were announced for 1937.

One feature per Act is the whole game: 1773 Supreme Court (Hastings first Governor-General), 1858 Crown rule and the Viceroy, 1909 separate electorates conceded, 1919 some representation in provincial assemblies, 1935 provincial autonomy.
